You are an expert in causal inference. The following question is not a typical commonsense query, but rather a meticulously designed question created by a professor specializing in causal inference, intended to assess the students' mastery of the course content.
Imagine a self-contained, hypothetical world with only the following conditions, and without any unmentioned factors or causal relationships: Gender has a direct effect on smoking and lung cancer. Smoking has a direct effect on tar deposit. Tar deposit has a direct effect on lung cancer. Gender is unobserved. Method 1: We look directly at how smoking correlates with lung cancer in general. Method 2: We look at this correlation case by case according to gender. To understand how smoking affects lung cancer, is it more correct to use the Method 1 than Method 2?
Start your answer with 'Yes' or 'No', followed by additional reasoning or evidence to support your explanation.

trace.content:
No, it is not more correct to use Method 1 than Method 2.

In this hypothetical world, we have a classic case of confounding by an unobserved variable (gender) that affects both the exposure (smoking) and the outcome (lung cancer). When we look directly at the correlation between smoking and lung cancer in general (Method 1), we are not accounting for the effect of gender on both variables. This can lead to biased estimates of the effect of smoking on lung cancer.

On the other hand, when we look at the correlation case by case according to gender (Method 2), we are effectively controlling for the confounding effect of gender. By stratifying the data by gender, we can estimate the effect of smoking on lung cancer within each gender group, which can provide a more accurate estimate of the causal relationship.

In particular, if we assume that the effect of smoking on lung cancer is the same across genders (a reasonable assumption given the direct effect of smoking on tar deposit and the direct effect of tar deposit on lung cancer), then the estimates from Method 2 will be more accurate than those from Method 1. This is because Method 2 is effectively accounting for the confounding effect of gender, which is a key principle in causal inference.

Therefore, in this hypothetical world, it is more correct to use Method 2 than Method 1 to understand how smoking affects lung cancer.
